title: Sampling from your beliefs
objectives: Build a Thompson sampling agent from Beta posteriors and compare three agents' regret.

screens.title: A belief per arm
screens.prose: Venue A has filled 7 of 10 orders and venue B 30 of 50. Give each a uniform prior, $\mathrm{Beta}(1, 1)$. As in `estimation`, $k$ wins in $n$ update it to $\mathrm{Beta}(1 + k, 1 + n - k)$, with mean $\tfrac{1 + k}{2 + n}$.
screens.question: What is the posterior mean of A's fill chance? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the first Beta parameter by the sum of both.

byKey.raw: That is the raw rate 7 of 10. The prior adds one win and one loss.
byKey.b: That is B's posterior mean. The question asks about A.
byKey.one-side: You added the prior's win but not its loss: $\tfrac{8}{11}$. The mean is $\tfrac{8}{8 + 4}$.

explain.text: $\mathrm{Beta}(8, 4)$ has mean $\tfrac{8}{12} = 0.6667$, and $\mathrm{Beta}(31, 21)$ has mean $\tfrac{31}{52} = 0.5962$. A looks better, but on far less evidence. The next screen shows how much less.

screens.title: Wide and narrow beliefs
screens.prose: The curves are the two posteriors. B's is fixed at $\mathrm{Beta}(31, 21)$. Slide A's fills out of its 10 orders and watch its curve move.

derive.caption: A: {{round(k)}} fills of 10, so Beta({{1 + round(k)}}, {{11 - round(k)}}).

screens.question: With A at 7 fills of 10, which posterior is wider?

options.text: A's, because it rests on 10 orders against B's 50
B's, because its mean is lower than A's
options.why: A lower mean does not widen a curve. The width shrinks with the number of orders, and B has 50.

options.text: They are the same width at 7 fills
options.why: Compare the spreads: A's curve spans roughly 0.4 to 0.9, B's roughly 0.45 to 0.73.

options.text: A's, because its mean is the higher one
options.why: A's mean is higher, but that moves the curve sideways. It is wider because it rests on 10 orders, not 50.

feedback.correct: A's curve is wide: 10 orders leave a lot of doubt.
feedback.generic: Compare how far each curve spreads along the $p$ axis.

explain.text: A's posterior rests on 10 orders, so it spreads from about 0.4 to 0.9. B's rests on 50 and is much narrower. A plausible draw from A can land below B, or far above it.

screens.title: Draw, then pull
screens.prose: **Thompson sampling** draws one fill chance from each posterior and pulls the arm with the larger draw. So it pulls A with the chance that A's draw beats B's. Numerical integration gives $P(\text{draw}_A > \text{draw}_B) = 0.6921$ for these two posteriors.
screens.question: What share of its next few pulls does Thompson sampling send to A, as a percentage to the nearest whole number?

widget.accept: 69%, the chance that A is the better venue

hints.text: Thompson pulls A exactly when A's draw is the larger.
That chance is given in the prose.

feedback.correct: About 69%: A gets the pull with the chance that it is the better venue.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Thompson pulls A whenever A's draw beats B's.

byKey.all: You pulled A every time because its mean is higher. Thompson pulls it only when its draw is higher.
byKey.half: The draws are not a coin flip: A's posterior sits mostly to the right of B's.
byKey.mean: That is A's posterior mean. The pull share is the chance A's draw beats B's, 0.6921.

explain.text: A's draw beats B's with chance 0.6921, so A gets about 69% of the pulls. This is **probability matching**: each arm is pulled with the chance that it is the best one.

screens.title: One more order
screens.prose: Thompson sends the next order to A, and it does not fill. Only A's posterior changes: a loss adds 1 to its second parameter.
screens.question: What is A's posterior mean now? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the miss to A's second parameter, then take the mean.

byKey.win: You added a win. The order did not fill, so the loss count goes up.
byKey.same: That is the mean before the order. The miss moves it.
byKey.raw: That is the raw rate 7 of 11. The prior's win and loss still count.

explain.text: A miss makes A's posterior $\mathrm{Beta}(8, 5)$, mean $\tfrac{8}{13} = 0.6154$. Its curve shifts left and narrows a little, so A's share of pulls falls. Each pull updates one belief, which steers the next draw.

screens.prose: Each pull: draw `rng.betavariate(1 + wins[i], 1 + losses[i])` for every arm in order, pick the first index of the largest draw, then `pull(ps[a], rng)`. Add the result to that arm's wins or losses. Return the total reward and the pulls per arm.

widget.solution:
import random

def pull(p, rng):
    return 1 if rng.random() < p else 0

def run_thompson(ps, T, seed):
    """Thompson sampling with Beta(1, 1) priors. Return (total reward, pulls per arm)."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    k = len(ps)
    wins = [0] * k
    losses = [0] * k
    total = 0
    for _ in range(T):
        draws = [rng.betavariate(1 + wins[i], 1 + losses[i]) for i in range(k)]
        a = draws.index(max(draws))
        r = pull(ps[a], rng)
        if r:
            wins[a] += 1
        else:
            losses[a] += 1
        total += r
    return total, [w + l for w, l in zip(wins, losses)]

hints.text: Keep win and loss counts per arm; the posteriors are built from them.
Draw for every arm before you pull.

feedback.correct: It matches. Most pulls go to C, with B checked now and then.
feedback.generic: Some tests fail. Draw for all arms first, in order, then pull once.

explain.text: The draws do all the exploring: a wide posterior sometimes throws out a high draw, so an uncertain arm still gets pulls. As an arm's record grows its draws cluster near its mean, and it is chosen only when it really looks best.

screens.title: Four agents, same seeds
screens.prose: We ran four agents on the three venues with seeds 0 to 199, 1,000 pulls each. The lines are the mean regret so far.
screens.question: Which agent has the lowest mean regret after 1,000 pulls?

options.text: Thompson sampling, at about 20.8
Epsilon-greedy, at about 24.0
options.why: Close, but its line ends above Thompson's. Its random pulls keep costing at the floor rate.

options.text: UCB1, at about 37.8
options.why: UCB1's worst-case bonus over-explores these close venues. Its line ends well above two others.

options.text: Greedy, at about 61.8
options.why: Greedy ends highest: it locked onto a worse venue in most seeds.

hints.text: Read where each line ends at 1,000 pulls.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the four end points.

explain.text: The end points are 61.8 for greedy, 37.8 for UCB1, 24.0 for epsilon-greedy and 20.8 for Thompson. Thompson spends its exploring where the posteriors are still wide. Its curve is also bending flat, unlike epsilon-greedy's.

screens.title: Random on purpose
screens.prose: A colleague reviews the agent. "A has the higher posterior mean, yet Thompson sends 31% of orders to B. It is flipping coins. Greedy would never waste an order like that."
screens.question: What is wrong with the colleague's argument?

options.text: The randomness is the exploring, and it is spent where the posteriors are wide
Nothing: removing the randomness would lower regret
options.why: Removing it gives greedy, the worst of the four at 61.8. The draws are what stop a lock-in on a lucky start.

options.text: Thompson only did well because the seeds were lucky
options.why: All four agents ran on the same 200 seeds. The gap is not luck.

options.text: Nothing much: random and greedy agents do about equally well
options.why: Greedy's 61.8 is three times Thompson's 20.8 on the same seeds.

hints.text: Ask what greedy would do with A after one bad run.
B's draws beat A's only when B might really be better.
Compare greedy's regret with Thompson's on the bars.

feedback.correct: The coin flips are weighted by the evidence: they are exploration with a purpose.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what the draws do that greedy cannot.

byKey.agree: You took randomness as waste. Without it you have greedy, which locks onto a worse arm in most seeds.

explain.text: Thompson pulls B exactly as often as B might be the better venue. As evidence piles up that chance shrinks and so does B's share. Greedy has no such check and paid 61.8 against 20.8.

screens.title: A stubborn prior
screens.prose: Someone seeds venue A with a strong prior, $\mathrm{Beta}(50, 10)$, from a vendor's brochure. Its mean is 0.8333. A truly fills with chance 0.45. After 100 orders it has filled 45.
screens.question: What is A's posterior mean after the 100 orders? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the 100 results to the prior's parameters.

byKey.flat: That is the mean from a flat prior, $\tfrac{46}{102}$. This prior counts as 60 orders already seen.
byKey.data: That is the data alone. The prior still holds 60 pseudo-orders.
byKey.prior: That is the prior mean. The 100 orders pull it down.

explain.text: The prior acts like 60 orders already seen, 50 of them fills. After 100 real orders the mean is $\tfrac{95}{160} = 0.5938$, still well above 0.45, so Thompson keeps over-sending to A. A strong wrong prior delays learning.

screens.title: Probability matching
screens.prose: Thompson sampling keeps a posterior per arm and, each pull, draws one value from each and pulls the largest. So $$P(\text{pull } a) = P(a \text{ is best} \mid \text{data}).$$ For 0 or 1 rewards with $\mathrm{Beta}(1, 1)$ priors, arm $a$ draws from $\mathrm{Beta}(1 + \text{wins}_a, 1 + \text{losses}_a)$.
screens.question: As an arm's record grows, what happens to the chance that Thompson pulls it, if it is not the best arm?

options.text: It falls towards 0 as its posterior narrows below the best arm's
It stays fixed, like epsilon-greedy's random share
options.why: Epsilon-greedy's share is fixed. Thompson's depends on the posteriors, which narrow with evidence.

options.text: It rises, because the arm has been tried more
options.why: More trials narrow the posterior around its true mean, below the best arm's, so its draws rarely win.

options.text: It settles near one half
options.why: One half would mean the arm is as likely to be best as not. Evidence says otherwise.

feedback.correct: Its chance of being best shrinks, so its share of pulls does too.
feedback.generic: Think about how the posterior of a worse arm changes with more data.

screens.title: Capital for new strategies
screens.prose: A fund trials new strategies with small capital and counts winning days. Strategy S has won 12 of 20 days; strategy T, launched later, 5 of 8. Each day the fund backs the strategy whose Thompson draw is larger, from $\mathrm{Beta}(1, 1)$ priors.
screens.question: What is T's posterior mean? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: $\mathrm{Beta}(6, 4)$ has mean 0.6, against S's $\tfrac{13}{22} = 0.5909$. Integration gives T the next day with chance 0.5276.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add T's winning days to the first parameter and its losing days to the second.

byKey.raw: That is the raw 5 of 8. The prior adds a win and a loss.

explain.text: T's posterior is $\mathrm{Beta}(6, 4)$, mean 0.6, only a little above S's 0.5909 and much wider. So T wins the draw with chance 0.5276: it gets capital often enough to prove itself, and S is not starved.

ideas: Keep a posterior per arm: with 0 or 1 rewards and a $\mathrm{Beta}(1, 1)$ prior, $\mathrm{Beta}(1 + \text{wins}, 1 + \text{losses})$.
Thompson sampling draws once from each posterior and pulls the largest draw, so each arm is pulled with the chance that it is the best.
Its randomness is the exploring, spent where beliefs are wide. On the venues, over seeds 0 to 199, it beat epsilon-greedy, UCB1 and greedy. A strong wrong prior delays it.

formula.name: Probability matching
formula.note: Each pull draws $\tilde p_a \sim \mathrm{Beta}(1 + w_a, 1 + l_a)$ and plays $\arg\max_a \tilde p_a$.

summary.trap: Thinking the random draws make Thompson worse than greedy. Greedy has no randomness and the worst regret; the draws are what keep a worse-looking arm under review.

quiz.prose: An arm starts at $\mathrm{Beta}(2, 2)$ and then wins 3 of 5 pulls.
quiz.question: What is its posterior mean? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add 3 wins and 2 losses to $\mathrm{Beta}(2, 2)$.

byKey.raw: That is the raw 3 of 5. The prior counts too.
byKey.flat: You used a $\mathrm{Beta}(1, 1)$ prior. This one starts at $\mathrm{Beta}(2, 2)$.

quiz.prose: Under Thompson sampling with two arms, the chance that arm X's draw beats arm Y's is 0.85.
quiz.question: What does that tell you?

options.text: X gets about 85% of the next pulls, for now
X's posterior mean is 0.85, its best guess
options.why: 0.85 is a chance about two draws, not X's mean. X's mean could be 0.4.

options.text: X will be pulled on every pull from now on
options.why: Y still wins 15% of the draws, so it keeps getting some pulls.

options.text: X's true value is higher, with certainty
options.why: It is the posterior chance that X is better, 0.85, not a certainty.

feedback.correct: Probability matching: each arm is pulled with the chance it is best.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask how often X's draw is the larger.

explain.text: Thompson pulls X whenever its draw is larger, which happens with chance 0.85. So X gets about 85% of pulls while the posteriors stay put.

quiz.prose: A prior $\mathrm{Beta}(30, 10)$ is placed on an arm.
quiz.question: How many observed pulls is that prior worth?

feedback.generic: Not quite. A $\mathrm{Beta}(a, b)$ prior counts as $a + b$ pulls.

byKey.wins: That is the pseudo-wins. Add the 10 pseudo-losses.
byKey.extra: You took off the uniform prior's 2. Count $a + b$ as in `estimation`.

explain.text: A $\mathrm{Beta}(a, b)$ prior acts like $a + b$ pulls already seen. So $\mathrm{Beta}(30, 10)$ is worth 40, and real data needs about that many pulls to outweigh it.
